summary: Flame in Freefall is a web platform for exploring and understanding scientific knowledge about combustion in microgravity. It features an interactive knowledge graph that visualizes connections between research, concepts and applications, alongside an AI-powered chatbot that answers natural-language questions using verifiable scientific sources. The platform transforms complex scientific information into accessible knowledge, supporting research, learning and fire safety applications both in space and on Earth.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web platform for exploring and understanding scientific knowledge about combustion in microgravity. It brings together the 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository: flight experiments such as ACME, FLEX, BASS, SAME and Saffire, plus their ground-based companion studies.

What it does and how it works: the platform has four sections. The Knowledge Graph is an interactive network that visualizes connections between investigations, hardware, fuels, measured values, scientific findings and real spacecraft fire incidents, from Apollo 1 to Artemis II. The Chatbot is an AI assistant that answers natural-language questions by querying that graph; every answer cites the NASA reports and papers it comes from, so users can verify it. Values compares test conditions and measured flammability parameters across investigations. On Earth explains how these results apply to fire safety at home, such as water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection and firefighter equipment. Behind the scenes, a data pipeline cataloged the PSI metadata and files, cleaned and standardized the experimental tables, and extracted findings from NASA final reports, fact sheets and technical papers. Each finding is stored with a verbatim quote from its source document.

Benefits and intended impact: microgravity combustion data is valuable but scattered across thousands of files, inconsistent metadata and long technical reports. Flame in Freefall turns that complex information into accessible, traceable knowledge. Researchers can find relevant experiments and compare results quickly, students and educators can learn how fire behaves without gravity, and engineers can connect experimental evidence to fire-safety decisions for spacecraft, lunar and Mars habitats, and buildings on Earth.

Tools and technologies: Python 3.12 (pandas, NetworkX) for the data pipeline; FastAPI for the backend; Neo4j as the graph database; the OpenAI API (GPT-6 Luna and text-embedding-3-large) for the GraphRAG chatbot; React 19, TypeScript and Vite for the frontend, with react-force-graph for the graph visualization; Poppler to extract text from PDFs; the OpenAlex API for scientific abstracts; and Docker for deployment. No special hardware was required.

Creativity: instead of a static dashboard, the project treats NASA's combustion research as a connected body of knowledge. Linking experiments to real fire incidents shows why each experiment matters for crew safety, and grounding every chatbot answer in quoted sources makes the AI useful for science rather than only conversational.

Factors we considered: scientific accuracy and traceability (answers must point to their sources); data quality (we documented inconsistencies in the PSI metadata and validated units and values); scope (we used PSI's official Combustion Science filter instead of a free-text search, which also returns non-combustion studies); responsible use of AI (a read-only database, query time limits and rate limiting for the chatbot); and accessibility for non-expert audiences.
